source.title: An open problem: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare in asynchronous Boolean networks?

accepted.question_text: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare under asynchronous update in Boolean networks, where a Boolean network is a discrete dynamical system whose variables are ON/OFF, asynchronous update changes one variable per time step, attractors are terminal recurrent state sets, minimal trap spaces are inescapable subspaces of the state space, and a motif-avoidant attractor is a complex attractor that lies outside every minimal trap space? The explanation should account for real-world biological Boolean networks, sparse and dense random Boolean networks, the role of input-node canalization, and why the observed hints do not yet yield a complete computational characterization of motif avoidance.

evidence.quote: An open problem: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare in asynchronous Boolean networks?

Despite recent efforts [21, 22], motif-avoidant attractors (MAAs) are still poorly understood, especially under asynchronous update. Empirical evidence suggests that motif-avoidant attractors are exceedingly rare in real-world biological networks [11, 23], but to the best of our knowledge, this observation has not been quantified before.
These hints do not yet give the whole picture, but they may point the way to a more complete understanding and computationally efficient characterization of motif avoidance.

accepted.question_text: What simple structural or dynamical criteria can determine the presence or absence of motif-avoidant attractors in asynchronously updated Boolean networks, beyond currently known sufficient exclusions such as interaction graphs with no cycles, only positive cycles, only negative cycles, no relevant path from a positive cycle to a negative cycle, or an L-cuttable interaction graph? Such criteria should handle dense networks, monotone or nested-canalizing update functions, and networks without negative self-regulation, because several natural candidate criteria fail on explicit counterexamples.

evidence.quote: We dedicated a significant effort to identifying conditions that guarantee or rule out motif avoidance. In the next section, we present a sampling of examples to illustrate the challenges of this investigation.
The search for simple criteria for the presence or absence of motif avoidance should continue.

These criteria leave many possibilities, especially in dense networks, in which motif avoidance cannot be ruled out. We considered several natural candidates for additional criteria on the structure of the interaction network, or on the Boolean update functions and found counterexamples for them.

accepted.question_text: How does node deletion reduction or model compression change motif avoidance in Boolean networks, and which conditions determine whether deleting non-self-regulating variables creates a new motif-avoidant attractor, destroys an existing motif-avoidant attractor by creating a stable motif or minimal trap space, or changes the network without producing motif avoidance? The question should cover both biological Boolean model reductions and random Boolean network reductions, because reduction can increase density and alter reachability in non-local ways.

evidence.quote: As we have seen, node deletion can, in practice, lead to the introduction of MAAs.
The emergence of these motif-avoidant attractors motivates further study into the relationship between node deletion and motif avoidance.

Our analysis demonstrates that even though motif-avoidant attractors are extremely rare in both biological and random networks, network reduction does meaningfully alter the likelihood of their presence.
Our results caution against the indiscriminate use of compression during modeling.

accepted.question_text: What is the minimal number and placement of linear extensions, equivalently delay nodes inserted on directed regulatory edges, needed to eliminate a given motif-avoidant attractor in an asynchronously updated Boolean network? The answer should sharpen the known sufficient strategy of delaying enough edges to make the interaction graph L-cuttable, explain when the upper bound based on network size N, number d of oscillating variables, and minimal disagreement m can be lowered, and characterize classes of motif-avoidant attractors for which one delay or many delays are necessary.

evidence.quote: Motivated by this observation, we sought to investigate the related questions of what makes motif avoidance appear and what is the minimal number of delays that eliminates a motif-avoidant attractor.

This algorithm yields an upper bound on the number of delays: (N −d)(N −1) +m(m+ 1)/2, where N is the number of variables, d ≤ N is the number of nodes that oscillate in the MAA, and m < d represents the minimal disagreement between a state of the MAA with (the fixed nodes of) the trap space, when considering only the oscillating nodes of the MAA.

We expect that the upper bound for the number of delays necessary to eliminate an MAA can be lowered in the classes of motif-avoidant attractors in which this issue can be ruled out; this may include all MAAs.

accepted.question_text: How common is the memory-state unreachability obstruction in delay-expanded Boolean networks, and under what conditions does it prevent a delay-based path from a motif-avoidant attractor to an avoided trap space? Here a canonical state is a delay-expanded state in which each delay node matches its parent node, a memory state is a state in which at least one delay node remembers a previous parent value, and the parameter m is the minimal disagreement between a state of the motif-avoidant attractor and the fixed nodes of the avoided trap space among the attractor's oscillating nodes.

evidence.quote: We discovered that the general reachability of memory states is not guaranteed. The reason for the loss of reachability is the loss of transitions in certain memory states compared to the original system (and to canonical states).

Significant open questions remain. For example, at present, there is no estimate of the prevalence of the unreachability issue (Appendix A.3) that limits the candidates for linear extensions to regulations of the trap space.
At present there is no estimate of the likelihood of a memory state needed to create a path to the trap space being unreachable from the motif-avoidant attractor.
If in fact it is true that unreachability only occurs for m = 1, then this issue does not pose a problem to MAA elimination.

accepted.question_text: Which explicit regulatory delays in biological Boolean network models affect long-term dynamics enough to change the biological interpretation of motif-avoidant attractors, and how should modelers decide which edge delays to include when building more realistic asynchronous Boolean models? This includes determining whether a motif-avoidant attractor is an artifact of instantaneous propagation along regulatory edges or a biologically meaningful oscillatory phenotype.

evidence.quote: Increased clarity on the minimal number of delays to eliminate a motif-avoidant attractor will help with the biological interpretation of motif avoidance.

MAAs under asynchronous or random set update retain an element of synchronicity: the effect of a variable’s state change is immediately reflected in all update functions it regulates. Though this may be a useful approximation in many cases, it fails to account for inherent delays in a system, such as when a protein must slowly diffuse through the cytoplasm to reach its target.
Identifying which delays affect the long-term dynamics of a Boolean network would be useful in building more biologically realistic models.
